---
title: "Slides, books & sites"
---

One block model drives several outputs. The same `.qmd` you preview as a page can
become a slide deck, and pointing the tool at a directory turns it into a book or
a whole website.

## Slide decks

Set `format: revealjs` and the document becomes a slide deck driven by qmd-fast's
**own engine** (no reveal.js, no CDN, everything bundled offline). `##` starts a
slide and `#` starts a section that nests the following slides as a vertical stack;
a title slide is generated from the metadata. The block diff still applies *within
the current slide*, so a live edit re-renders one block without resetting your
position, and Alt-clicking (Option-clicking on Mac) a block jumps to its source,
exactly like a page.

```sh
qmd-fast preview docs/guide/demo.qmd   # live, click-to-source, hot reload
qmd-fast build   docs/guide/demo.qmd   # one self-contained .html
```

The engine ships the things you actually present with, and the demo deck embedded
further down this page puts each one on its own slide. The rest of this section is the
exact authoring syntax for those features. (The deck's source lives at
`docs/guide/demo.qmd`, so you can read it side by side with these snippets.)

### Reveal content step by step

Two ways to stage a slide, both standard Markdown-in-a-fence:

```markdown
::: {.incremental}
- This bullet shows first
- then this one
- then this one
:::
```

`::: {.incremental}` turns each list item into its own step. For finer control, mark
any single block `.fragment` and it reveals on its own click. To split a slide into
two halves at an arbitrary point, drop a line that is only `. . .` (three
dots, spaces between them):

```markdown
## A two-beat slide

Here is the setup, visible immediately.

. . .

And here is the payoff, revealed on the next click.
```

The pause marker is dropped from the output and everything after it (until the next
pause or the end of the slide) becomes a fragment, so the audience reads the setup,
then you click for the punchline.

### Step through code line by line

Put a `code-line-numbers` attribute on a fenced code block (note the leading dot on
the language, the deck's display form for a non-executing block):

````markdown
```{.python code-line-numbers="1|2-3|4"}
import numpy as np
x = np.linspace(0, 1, 100)
y = np.sin(2 * np.pi * x)
print(y.max())
```
````

The `|`-separated segments are the steps: `1`, then `2-3`, then `4`. Each segment is a
line spec (`3`, `3-5`, `1,4`, or `all`); the lines in the current segment are
highlighted and the rest dim. The first segment is the slide's resting state, applied
before you take any step, so segment `1` above is lit the moment the slide appears.

### Magic-move between code snapshots

Wrap two or more consecutive code blocks in `::: {.magic-move}` and the deck tweens
between them: lines with matching text glide to their new position, new lines fade in,
removed lines fade out. Each block-to-block hop is one step.

````markdown
::: {.magic-move}
```python
def area(r):
    return 3.14 * r * r
```

```python
import math

def area(r):
    return math.pi * r ** 2
```
:::
````

### Auto-animate matched elements

Give two consecutive slides the same `auto-animate` attribute and the engine morphs
matched elements (by tag and text) from their place on the first slide to their place
on the second: a heading slides up, a code block grows, an image moves. Reusing the
same `##` title across both is the usual trick (the deck dedupes the slide ids for
you, so the repeat does not collide):

```markdown
## One source, many views {auto-animate=true}

The same `.qmd` renders as a page, a book, a website, or this deck.

## One source, many views {auto-animate=true}

The same `.qmd` renders as a page, a book, a website, or this deck.

> The title above tweened into place.
```

Unmatched elements just appear; matched ones tween.

### Per-slide backgrounds

Set a background on the slide's heading and the engine hoists it onto the slide and
flips the text to light when the backdrop is dark:

```markdown
## On a dark panel {background-color="#0f172a"}

## With a gradient {background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg,#4c6ef5,#9775fa)"}

## Over a photo {background-image="cover.jpg"}
```

`background-image` also accepts companion attributes for the layer:
`background-size` (default `cover`), `background-position` (default `center`), and
`background-repeat` (default `no-repeat`). A background travels with its slide as the
camera pans and shows as a per-tile backdrop in the overview.

### Vertical stacks

A `#` (section) heading opens a vertical stack and the `##` slides that follow nest
under it; the audience presses <kbd>↓</kbd> to go deeper and <kbd>→</kbd> to move on
to the next topic. So a section can carry its own thread without cluttering the main
left-to-right flow.

```markdown
# A topic with depth

## The headline point

## A supporting sub-slide
```

### Stretch an image to fit

Wrap an image in `::: {.r-stretch}` and it grows to fill the slide's leftover vertical
space (aspect ratio preserved), so a chart or screenshot is not left tiny under a
heading.

```markdown
## A chart that fills the slide

::: {.r-stretch}
![](chart.svg)
:::
```

### Present, export, and annotate

These are all keyboard / menu actions on a running deck (every one is also in the
corner control menu, opened with <kbd>m</kbd> or <kbd>?</kbd>, so nothing is
keyboard-only):

| Key | Action |
|---|---|
| <kbd>→</kbd> / <kbd>Space</kbd> | Next step or slide |
| <kbd>←</kbd> | Previous |
| <kbd>↑</kbd> / <kbd>↓</kbd> | Jump to the topic above / below (vertical stacks) |
| <kbd>o</kbd> / <kbd>Esc</kbd> | Overview: a zoomable map of every slide (press <kbd>/</kbd> to filter by title) |
| <kbd>s</kbd> | Speaker view (see below) |
| <kbd>f</kbd> | Fullscreen |
| <kbd>d</kbd> | Drawing mode: a pen to annotate the current slide (colours, eraser, clear) |
| <kbd>b</kbd> / <kbd>.</kbd> | Black the screen mid-talk; any of <kbd>b</kbd>/<kbd>.</kbd>/<kbd>Esc</kbd> restores it |
| <kbd>Ctrl/Cmd-P</kbd> | Export PDF (one clean slide per page) |

**Speaker view** (<kbd>s</kbd>) opens a second window showing the current and next
slide as live previews, the current slide's speaker notes, and a running timer plus a
clock. Write notes in a `::: {.notes}` block on the slide and they appear only in the
speaker window:

```markdown
## A slide with notes

The audience sees this.

::: {.notes}
Only you see this, in speaker view. Remember to slow down here.
:::
```

The two windows stay in sync over the local connection (it even works from a built
`file://` deck), and either window can drive the navigation.

**Reader mode** is the default when you open a deck as a link: it flattens to a
scrollable, full-width reading column (set in the reading serif) with every fragment
shown, since that is how a reader meets the deck on their own. It is also automatic on a
narrow or portrait screen, where the fixed-aspect deck would letterbox badly. To
**present** the stepped deck instead, open it with `?qmd=present` (or `?qmd=slides`); you
can also switch modes from the control menu, and `?qmd=scroll` always forces reader mode.

**Live code and `{js}`** work in a deck exactly as on a page: `{python}` / `{r}` cells
execute against the warm kernel and native `{js}` cells stay interactive, right on the
slide. See [Executable content](code.qmd) and [Interactive documents](interactive.qmd).

### Embedding a deck in a page

`{{< embed deck.qmd >}}` drops a deck into any page or chapter as an isolating,
interactive iframe with a fullscreen button, so an article can lead with a swipeable
summary or a site can showcase a live demo. The referenced deck is built and served
automatically alongside the page. Here is this manual's own feature deck:

## Books and a live table of contents

A document with `toc: true` gains a table of contents built from its heading
anchors and rebuilt live as you edit, with the current section highlighted as you
scroll (a scrollspy). On a wide screen it's a sticky sidebar; on a phone it
collapses into a pull-up sheet.

A **multi-chapter book** is a directory whose `_site.yml` lists `chapters:`:
their presence makes it a book (no `type:` needed), optionally grouped into
`part:`s. qmd-fast numbers the chapters, builds the left sidebar, wires prev/next
navigation, and resolves cross-references across chapters. *These very docs are
such a book*: look at the sidebar and press <kbd>Cmd/Ctrl-K</kbd> to search.

```yaml
title: "My Book"
toc: true
chapters:
  - index.qmd
  - part: "Part One"
    chapters: [a.qmd, b.qmd]
```

## Multi-page websites

Point either command at a **directory** and qmd-fast treats it as a website
project. The directory needs one root config, `_site.yml`, which names the site
title, the navbar, and the footer; every `.qmd` under it (skipping `_`-prefixed
partials) becomes a page.

```yaml
title: "My Site"
favicon: favicon.svg
nav:
  - { text: Blog, href: blog.qmd }
  - { text: Projects, href: projects.qmd }
footer:
  left: "© 2026 Me"
  right:
    - { icon: github, href: "https://github.com/me" }
```

```sh
qmd-fast build   corpus/tech-blog     # static site -> _site/ (deployable)
qmd-fast preview corpus/tech-blog     # live site on http://127.0.0.1:4321
```

See the [configuration reference](../reference/configuration.qmd) for every key
(and the note on migrating a Quarto-shaped config by flattening it to the native
schema).

`build` writes one `.html` per page (mirroring the input tree) and copies the
referenced assets, so the output folder deploys as-is. `preview` serves the same
site **live**: the navbar links navigate between pages (each a real
page load with its own websocket), and the page you are editing hot-reloads in
place. Intra-site `.qmd` links (including `other-page.qmd#anchor`) are rewritten to
their `.html` targets automatically.

To ship a website and a separate docs **book** as one deploy, build the book into a
subfolder of the site's output with `--out`, then link to it from the navbar:

```sh
qmd-fast build my-site                 # -> my-site/_site/
qmd-fast build docs --out my-site/_site/docs   # the book, nested at /docs
# navbar:  - { text: Docs, href: docs/index.html }
```

Config is **two levels, no cascade**: the root `_site.yml` sets project-wide
defaults and a page's own front matter overrides them. There is deliberately no
Quarto-style `_metadata.yml` directory merge, the single most confusing part of
its model.

Three front-matter blocks generate whole page sections so you do not hand-write the
chrome: `hero:` (a landing header), `about:` (a profile header), and `listing:` (an
index that crawls a directory). All three are page front matter, documented in full in
the [front-matter reference](../reference/frontmatter.qmd); the practical shapes
follow.

### A landing header with `hero:`

`hero:` builds a centered landing band: an optional small uppercase `eyebrow:` kicker,
a big `headline:` (it falls back to the page `title:` when omitted), a supporting
`lead:` sentence, and a row of call-to-action buttons. Mark one button
`primary: true` to render it as the filled accent button; the rest are outlined.

```yaml
title: "My Project"
hero:
  eyebrow: "Open source"
  headline: "A faster way to publish"
  lead: "One source file, four output shapes, zero CDN."
  actions:
    - { text: "Get started", href: docs/index.html, primary: true }
    - { text: "Source", href: "https://github.com/me/proj" }
```

### A profile header with `about:`

`about:` builds a centered profile header (a round `image:`, the page `title:` as the
name, and a row of `links:`). The default `template:` is `jolla`, the centered style
the corpus uses; it is kept as a CSS class on the header so a theme can restyle it.

```yaml
title: "Jane Rivera"
about:
  template: jolla
  image: avatar.jpg
  image-alt: "Jane Rivera"
  links:
    - { text: GitHub, href: "https://github.com/jane", icon: github }
    - { text: Email, href: "mailto:jane@example.com", icon: email }
```

`hero:` and `about:` are alternative treatments of the same page header, so a page
declares one or the other (each replaces the title block; if both are somehow present,
`hero:` wins). Reach for `hero:` on a marketing or landing page where you want a
pitch plus buttons, and `about:` on a person-or-project page where you want an avatar
plus profile links.

### An index of pages with `listing:`

`listing:` turns a page into an index. It crawls the directory named by `contents:`
(relative to the page) and emits a card per document there, pulling each card's image,
date, title, description, and categories from that document's own front matter. So a
blog index, a projects index, or a homepage's "recent posts" all generate from front
matter, and adding a post is just adding a file.

```yaml
title: "Blog"
listing:
  contents: posts
  type: grid
  sort: "date desc"
  categories: true
  max-items: 12
```

The knobs:

- `contents:` (required) is the directory to list, relative to this page.
- `type: grid` renders a card grid with cover images; omit it (or any other value) for
  a stacked list without images.
- `sort:` orders by date. The default is `"date desc"` (newest first); use
  `"date asc"` for oldest first. (Any value containing `asc` sorts ascending;
  otherwise it is descending.)
- `max-items:` caps how many cards appear.
- `categories: true` adds a filter-chip row above the cards, one chip per category
  found across the listing (with a count), plus an "All" chip; clicking a chip filters
  the grid in the browser.

## Themes

`theme:` selects the built-in `light` (default) or `dark`, a `.css`/`.scss` file,
or an installed `_extensions/<name>/` bundle. A theme is just a `:root` block of
CSS custom properties (`--qmd-*`); the navbar, footer, callouts, diagrams, and
code all read those variables, so one small file restyles everything and the
light/dark toggle just swaps the values: nothing re-renders. The full list of
`--qmd-*` variables and how to author a theme is in [Theming](theming.qmd).

The `{{< embed >}}` shortcode used above, and its sibling `{{< video >}}`, are
documented in the [shortcodes reference](../reference/shortcodes.qmd).
